items.title: Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act Provisions; Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Framework Adjustment 7 to the Atlantic Spiny Dogfish Fishery Management Plan
items.content_text: NMFS proposes measures included in Framework Adjustment 7 to the Spiny Dogfish Fishery Management Plan (FMP), as recommended by the Mid-Atlantic and New England Fishery Management Councils. Framework 7 proposes fishing year 2026 and projected 2027 specifications, which would establish allowable harvest levels for the spiny dogfish fishery to prevent overfishing while enabling optimum yield based on the best scientific information available. Framework 7 also proposes changes to the Atlantic spiny dogfish accountability measures intended to provide the commercial fishery with greater flexibility by no longer requiring full payback of annual catch limit (ACL) overages when the Atlantic spiny dogfish stock is considered healthy.

items.title: Fisheries of the Northeastern United States; Summer Flounder Fishery; 2026 Commercial Quota Harvested for the State of Maine
items.content_text: NMFS announces that the 2026 summer flounder commercial quota allocated to the State of Maine has been harvested. Vessels issued a commercial Federal fisheries permit for the summer flounder fishery may not land summer flounder in Maine for the remainder of calendar year 2026, unless additional quota becomes available through a transfer from another state. Regulations governing the summer flounder fishery require publication of this notification to advise Maine that the quota has been harvested, and to advise vessel permit holders and dealer permit holders that no Federal commercial quota is available for landing summer flounder in Maine.

items.title: Energy Conservation Program: Test Procedures for Commercial Warm Air Furnaces
items.content_text: The Department of Energy ("DOE" or "the Department") is withdrawing the test procedure for commercial warm air furnaces adopted under the Energy Policy and Conservation Act, specifically appendix B, "Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency Two)." Upon reconsideration, DOE has determined that appendix B would have an uncertain increase in representativeness that does not outweigh the likely increase in burden. DOE has also determined that withdrawing the appendix B test procedure would be consistent with the proposed Process Rule, which states that for certain categories of equipment, including CWAFs, DOE will adopt the industry test procedure, as contemplated by EPCA, except in very limited circumstances. Commercial warm air furnaces will continue to be subject to the testing requirements of appendix A, "Uniform Test Method for Measurement of the Energy Efficiency of Commercial Warm Air Furnaces (Thermal Efficiency)."

Maine Forest Service report highlights effectiveness of forestry practices that protect water quality

October 1, 2026

AUGUSTA, Maine, October 1, 2026 - A new Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Maine Forest Service (MFS) report underscores the effectiveness of environmentally friendly practices during timber harvesting. Released Oct. 1, the "Maine Forestry Best Management Practices Use and Effectiveness Data Summary" draws on hundreds of observations at timber harvesting sites across Maine.

This MFS study shows how forestry and timber industry professionals use recommended practices statewide. It also demonstrates that the risk to waterbodies greatly increases when they are improperly applied.

These measures, called Best Management Practices (BMP), are voluntarily implemented by professionals to help protect water quality in Maine's streams, rivers, lakes, and wetlands. They cover planning and application recommendations for activities such as stream crossings, road construction, and controlling erosion and sediment, the primary pollutants associated with timber harvesting.

Maines forest industry has made great strides in protecting water resources in recent decades, said State Forester and MFS Director Patty Cormier. The improvements weve identified through our BMP monitoring program are a testament to the ongoing value of the training that loggers, foresters, and woodland owners have participated in and applied. We thank them, our training partners, and collaborators for their contributions to this progress.

The report, released every two years, is the result of this monitoring from 2024 to 2025. It includes data from 165 timber harvesting sites and observations on over 700 individual activities, including around stream crossings, contaminants, and log landing placement.

This year's key findings include:

  • 74% of study sites applied appropriate practices on stream crossings. In many cases, they included planning to avoid crossings altogether. MFS emphasizes avoiding stream crossings when possible because they present the highest risk for sedimentation.
  • Soil movement monitoring found that, in 85% of cases, no sediment entered a water body. Of the 15% instances where sediment was recorded, 9% were in measurable amounts (~1 cubic foot or more of sediment), and 6% were trace amounts.
  • 87% of sites showed no evidence of chemical spills, a 10% decrease from the previous report. Reported spills ranged from minor drips to less than 10 square feet.
  • Progress on improving fish passage continues. Although the number of stream-crossing structures adequately spanning stream channels on haul roads decreased by 5% since the previous report, adequate crossings on operation trails increased by 17%.

This year's results are largely consistent with previous reports and continue to show that Maine's forestry and logging communities are using BMPs effectively. BMP use and effectiveness at timber harvesting operations are monitored regularly by the MFS District Foresters and Water Resources Specialist. In addition, MFS staff provide regular training and support for their application, with presentations and workshops across the state.

Since 2000, MFS staff have conducted a systematic statewide monitoring program of BMPs on a sample of timber harvesting operations across the state. Support from Maine landowners, loggers, and foresters has been critical to its implementation and effectiveness. MFS efforts also include financial incentives for loggers and foresters to acquire temporary bridges, which are among the most effective measures to install stream crossings with minimal impact.

In the latest report, and throughout the programs history, monitoring shows that when sedimentation was observed, it was most often due to inadequate BMP application. The risk of detrimental impacts also greatly increases if they are not applied or applied incorrectly. Previous reports and numerous national studies have also documented that BMPs help protect water resources when properly applied. The latest findings reinforce that continued monitoring, education, and training are key to sustaining the success of forestry BMPs and their environmental benefits.

The report can be found on the MFS Forest Policy and Management Division website.

For more information contact: Fritz Freudenberger, MFS Division Communications Specialist at: Frederick.Freudenberger@Maine.gov (207) 441-2539

items.title: US Labor Department finds railroad illegally terminated employee who refused to work during severe weather
items.content_text: LITTLE ROCK, AR – A U.S. Department of Labor Occupational Safety and Health Administration whistleblower investigation has concluded that Union Pacific Railroad Co. violated the Federal Railroad Safety Act when it removed from service and later terminated a North Little Rock yardman who notified management of nearby lightning and federal safety standards. OSHA determined that the employee voiced concerns about nearby lightning, cited OSHA and NOAA lightening safety guidelines, initiated a safety stand-down, and refused to work until the storm passed. Within minutes of the stand-down, Union Pacific removed the employee from service and was later charged with insubordination. Union Pacific terminated his employment on May 30, 2024.On June 10, 2026, OSHA ordered Union Pacific to remove from the employee’s employment records any reference of the incident, and pay back wages, lost benefits, compensatory and punitive damages totaling at least $304,869, and attorney’s fees. Union Pacific filed objections to OSHA’s order and has requested a hearing before a U.S. Department of Labor Administrative Law Judge.OSHA’s Whistleblower Protection Program enforces 25 whistleblower statutes that protect employees from retaliation for reporting violations of workplace airline, anti-money laundering, commercial motor carrier, consumer product, criminal antitrust, environmental, financial reform, food safety, health insurance reform, maritime, motor vehicle safety, nuclear, pipeline, public transportation agency, railroad, safety and health, securities, and tax laws.Editor’s note: The U.S. Department of Labor does not release the names of employees involved in whistleblower complaints.

items.title: General Provisions; Revised List of Birds Protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act
items.content_text: We, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service), propose to revise the List of Birds Protected by the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) by both adding and removing species and changing names to conform to accepted use by the scientific community. Reasons for the proposed changes to the list include adding species based on new taxonomy and new evidence of natural occurrence in the United States or U.S. territories, removing species no longer known to occur within the United States or U.S. territories, and changing names to reflect currently accepted taxonomy and nomenclature. The net increase of 25 species (32 added and 7 removed) would bring the total number of species protected by the MBTA to 1,131. We also propose to revise the names of species subject to specific migratory bird permit regulations to reflect currently accepted taxonomy and nomenclature. We are taking this proposed action because an accurate and up-to-date list of species protected by the MBTA is essential for public notification, regulatory, and law-enforcement purposes, and to ensure consistency in the use of common and scientific names across Service regulations.

Sep 25, 2026

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) reminds Maine people and visitors to take steps to keep themselves, their loved ones, and neighbors healthy this respiratory virus season.

Respiratory viruses can cause fever, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle aches, and fatigue. Some people are more likely to get very sick and need medical attention. These viruses can spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes. They can also spread from touching the surface with the virus on it and then touching your nose or mouth before washing your hands.

The Maine CDC recommends the following measures to protect yourself and others:

  • Stay home when you are sick.
  • Wash your hands frequently with soap and water.
  • Clean and disinfect surfaces and objects that people touch often.
  • If you are sick, consider wearing a mask around others.
  • Cover coughs and sneezes with a tissue or your elbow.
  • Avoid close contact with people who are sick.
  • Get vaccinated, as appropriate for flu, COVID-19, and RSV.

Vaccination is the most effective way to prevent respiratory viruses. Vaccines can also help make illness less severe and help prevent missed work or school. Getting a flu vaccine every year and staying up to date with COVID-19 and RSV vaccinations, if eligible, can help lower the risk of getting sick.

Consistent with the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics, American Academy of Family Physicians, and American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Maine CDC recommends the following respiratory virus immunization for the 2026-2027 season:

  • Flu: Everyone 6 months and older should receive an annual flu vaccine.
  • COVID-19: Vaccination is recommended for
    • all children ages 6 through 23 months;
    • children and adolescents ages 2 through 18 years who are at increased risk for severe COVID-19 or who want to be vaccinated;
    • adults age 19 and older;
    • pregnant individuals.
  • RSV: Immunization is recommended for certain infants, pregnant people, and older adults.
    • Infants: RSV immunization is recommended for those younger than 8 months born during or entering their first RSV season, if they are not protected by maternal RSV vaccination.
      • Certain children ages 8-19 months who are at increased risk for severe RSV may also be recommended to receive RSV immunization during their second season.
    • Pregnant people: RSV vaccination is recommended during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy.
    • Older adults: All adults age 75 and older and adults 50-74 at increased risk for severe RSV illness.

To find the nearest location to get a vaccine, contact your local pharmacy or health care provider.

Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, when I took office nearly eight years ago, I promised that Maine won't wait to take action to protect our state, our people, and our economy from the dangers of extreme weather events caused by pollution and changes to our environment. And I promised that we would fight to preserve this special place that we call home; preserve it for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

The stakes could not be higher. Look no further than the devastating storms of just a few years ago. Storms that impacted our communities, our people, and our economy—that destroyed a lot of infrastructure across the state.

I've made climate action a cornerstone of my Administration. First, we created the Maine Climate Council, and we issued a groundbreaking climate action plan. And we dedicated millions of federal and state dollars to make that plan a reality.

In 2025, we made the single largest investment in storm recovery by any administration in Maine history, and we created the State Resilience Office to build better, stronger public infrastructure to withstand future storms.

That office manages a partnership of more than 300 communities and has awarded more than $29 million in state and federal funds for projects to prepare local communities for flooding, for storm surge, for rising sea levels, and other climate and weather events that put people's lives and livelihoods at risk.

Recently, I was proud to announce the latest round of funding through that partnership: more than $4.7 million in grants to 72 cities and Tribal Governments, including the towns of Bingham and Madawaska:

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;
  • And the Town of Freedom will use its grant to do an energy audit of its buildings and to plan for a bridge replacement across Hustus Brook.

Through these projects and so many more, we are continuing to address the very real threat of severe weather events for the health of our people, the health of our environment, and the health of our economy.

You know that clean air and clean water know no political party. Our planet is neither Democratic nor Republican. It's the home of all of us, and it is the responsibility of all of us and all governments to preserve it for future generations.

I am proud that over the past nearly eight years, we've made cost-effective heat pumps, weatherization programs, and other things available for Maine people and businesses. We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

We won't wait for the next storm or the next disaster. We do care. And as the author Wendell Berry wrote, "We care for this home that is ours. A home that we care for as we care for no other place in the world."

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

Sep 16, 2026

The Maine Department of Health and Human Services’ Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) is reporting a case of measles in Maine; the first case in the state since five cases were confirmed in February of this year. The Maine CDC confirmed the latest case on September 15, 2026. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (U.S. CDC), as of September 11, there were 3,294 confirmed measles cases reported nationwide in 2026.

The individual is an unvaccinated adult from Somerset County. The Maine CDC is working with the facility where potential exposure occurred and is working with them to inform potentially exposed individuals.

Individuals who were at the following location* during the timeframe listed below were potentially exposed to measles and should take precautions and should watch for symptoms for 21 days after September 12:

Location

Date

Time

MaineGeneral Express Care, Waterville 211 Main Street, Waterville, ME

September 12, 2026

8am-11am

*Subject to change as the investigation continues

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include:

  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes
  • Rash that spreads from the head down.

Individuals who develop symptoms should contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection. If symptoms are consistent with measles, a health care professional may test to determine a measles infection.

Measles can cause severe sickness including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain swelling), and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once infected, a person is contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. The period from exposure to onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but can be longer.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. Individuals who:   

  • have been potentially exposed should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms.
  • are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated.
  • develop symptoms should contact their health provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection.

Recommendations: 

  • Children – Identify and vaccinate children who are not up to date with their MMR vaccines. All children should receive two doses of MMR vaccine. A health care professional should administer the first dose to children at 12 to 15 months old and the second at 4 to 6 years old.
    • Children 6 to 11 months old who will be traveling internationally or domestically to a region with a known active measles outbreak should receive one dose of MMR vaccine, per the Maine CDC’s expanded recommendations for those traveling to a destination with a known outbreak. This dose is not considered part of the routine two-dose series starting at age 12 months.  
  • Adults – All adults should have proof of immunity to measles. Acceptable proof includes one of the following:
    • written documentation of vaccination
    • laboratory evidence of immunity
    • birth before 1957
    • or laboratory confirmation of disease
    • individuals who received a measles vaccine between 1963 to 1967 are encouraged to speak with their doctor to determine if additional vaccination is needed. Those known to have received an inactivated dose measles vaccine should receive a single dose of MMR. Five percent of people who received measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated vaccine.

For adults with no evidence of immunity to measles, the U.S. CDC recommends one dose of MMR vaccine as soon as possible. Adults who are traveling domestically or internationally to a region known to have an active measles outbreak should receive two doses of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive any live virus vaccine during pregnancy, including MMR.

Vaccination Information:

  • Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
  • The U.S. CDC considers people who received two doses of MMR vaccine as a child protected for life. 
  • Some people exposed to the virus may still get measles even if they got the MMR vaccine. In this case, they are more likely to have a milder illness and are also less likely to spread the disease to other people.

For More Information:

  • The Maine CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.maine.gov/dhhs/measles
  • The U.S. CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.cdc.gov/measles/index.html
  • The Maine Immunization Program webpage: https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/mecdc/infectious-disease/immunization/
